strengths: Clear and interesting central finding: L0 is not a free hyperparameter but has a 'correct' value determined by the true sparsity of underlying features, and deviating from it (in either direction) causes feature mixing/degeneracy. This challenges the common 'sparsity-reconstruction tradeoff' framing used broadly in the SAE literature.

The toy model experiments (Section 3, Figure 1, Appendix A.2/A.3) are well controlled with known ground truth, clearly demonstrating that low L0 causes correlated-feature mixing and that MSE actively rewards this incorrect solution over the ground-truth dictionary — a compelling and clean illustration of the core claim.

The proposed N-th decoder projection metric (s^dec_n) is a novel, simple, unsupervised diagnostic that requires no ground truth and is shown to be robust to choice of N in both toy and LLM settings (Figures 2, 3, 10).

The LLM validation on Gemma-2-2b connects the toy-model metric to a real downstream task (sparse probing F1), showing the metric's optimum coincides with peak probing performance (Figure 4), lending some external validity to the approach.

Practically relevant finding: survey of open-source SAEs on Neuronpedia (Appendix A.5) shows most public SAEs use L0 well below what the paper's analysis suggests is optimal, which if correct has significant implications for the community.

Honest and fairly detailed limitations section and inclusion of a preliminary automatic L0-tuning procedure (Appendix A.4) with discussion of its practical difficulties, showing methodological transparency.
weaknesses: The LLM-scale claim that 'true L0' is 200-250 rests entirely on a single model/layer (Gemma-2-2b, layer 12) and a single training distribution (The Pile), yet the paper generalizes broadly ('most SAEs used by researchers have L0 too low'); this is a substantial overreach given the narrow empirical base (explicitly acknowledged as a limitation, but the abstract/discussion still make strong general claims).

The core validation of 'correctness' on LLMs is indirect: there is no ground truth for true L0 in Gemma-2-2b, so the paper relies on (a) its own proposed metric and (b) sparse probing F1, which is itself a proxy with known caveats (probing performance need not equal correct disentangled feature recovery, especially since increasing L0 could simply give probes more capacity/parameters, akin to giving a probe more directions to work with regardless of feature correctness).

The toy model itself is fairly simple (50 orthogonal features, fixed correlation structure, single firing-magnitude distribution) and may not capture more complex phenomena like hierarchical/compositional features, feature splitting/absorption, or high-dimensional superposition regimes relevant to real LLMs — the mapping from toy model conclusions to LLM behavior is asserted rather than rigorously established.

No statistical uncertainty or repeated-seed analysis is reported; single-run toy model and single-run LLM sweep results are presented as if definitive, without error bars or robustness checks across random seeds, correlation matrices, or different layers/models.

The paper only studies BatchTopK SAEs (Appendix A.6 limitations acknowledges this) while claiming (without evidence) that findings generalize to L1/JumpReLU SAEs; this is an unverified extrapolation given these architectures set sparsity indirectly via loss coefficients and may behave differently.

The s^dec_n metric's practical utility for a practitioner is limited: the automatic L0-tuning procedure in Appendix A.4 is described as requiring heavy hyperparameter tuning and did not work robustly for LLMs, undermining the paper's practical actionability despite the strong prescriptive claims in the abstract ('practitioners must set L0 correctly').

The paper is quite short (4 main pages) with limited related work discussion and no comparison against alternative methods for choosing L0 (e.g., simple validation-based downstream task tuning, other proposed sparsity-selection heuristics), making it hard to assess the added value of s^dec_n over simpler baselines.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: code availability is mentioned but the repository link appears missing/empty in the text ('Our code is available at' with no URL), and specifics of correlation matrix generation, exact hyperparameters for LLM SAE training beyond learning rate, and compute budget are only partly specified.

strengths: The paper tackles a clearly articulated and practically relevant question (how to set L0 in SAEs) that most prior work treats as a free hyperparameter, and the toy-model demonstration with known ground-truth features is a clean, interpretable way to illustrate the feature-mixing phenomenon at both too-low and too-high L0.

The observation that MSE/reconstruction can be lower for an SAE with deliberately corrupted, polysemantic latents than for the ground-truth correct dictionary (Fig. 6, Fig. 7) is a compelling and concrete critique of the common 'sparsity-reconstruction tradeoff' framing used throughout the SAE literature.

The proposed Nth decoder projection score is a simple, computationally cheap diagnostic that does not require labeled probing data, and the paper shows a plausible correspondence between its minimum and peak sparse-probing F1 on a real LLM (Gemma-2-2b), which is an encouraging convergent validation across two very different signals.

The audit of open-source SAEs on Neuronpedia (Appendix A.5) is a useful, concrete contribution showing that widely used SAEs (across GPT-2, Gemma, Llama) have L0 values well below what the paper's analysis suggests is appropriate, giving the work practical relevance to the community.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is very narrow: all LLM experiments are on a single model (Gemma-2-2b), a single layer (layer 12), a single SAE width (32k), and a single architecture (BatchTopK). The strong, generalized claim in the abstract/title ('most commonly used SAEs have an L0 that is too low') is not adequately supported by evidence from only one layer of one model; no evidence is given that the L0=200-250 result, or even the qualitative phenomenon, transfers to other layers, model sizes, or architectures (L1, JumpReLU, TopK) despite the title's broad framing.

The toy model is extremely simple (50 orthogonal features in R^100, single random correlation matrix, single firing-probability schedule) and results are shown for a single random seed with no error bars or repeated trials across different correlation structures, feature counts, or dimensionalities. It is unclear how robust the qualitative conclusions (and the precise behavior of s^dec_n) are to this specific toy setup.

The 'ground truth' validation for the LLM setting is entirely indirect: the claimed optimal L0 is justified by correspondence with sparse-probing F1, a downstream proxy that could be influenced by many confounds (e.g., simply having a higher-capacity sparse code improves linear probe separability regardless of whether the 'true' L0 is being discovered). No independent, feature-level validation (e.g., human/autointerp monosemanticity assessment, synthetic feature recovery in a more realistic superposition setting) is provided for the LLM claims, leaving the central empirical claim about real SAEs weakly substantiated relative to the strength of the paper's conclusions.

The proposed automatic L0-selection procedure (Appendix A.4) is reported to work well on the toy model but to require extensive, unreported hyperparameter tuning in real LLMs and is not demonstrated to successfully converge on an LLM in the paper; this central practical payoff of the method is left essentially unresolved, undermining the actionable contribution promised by the abstract/discussion.

The metric s^dec_n itself is heuristic and its justification is informal (an intuitive argument about 'near-zero projections' rather than a derivation or theoretical guarantee); the choice of n is shown empirically to shift the slope/shape of the curve, and no principled guidance is given for selecting n in practice beyond 'about h/2', which limits reproducibility and practical applicability.

Much of the conceptual contribution (correlated features causing mixing at low sparsity) overlaps substantially with cited prior work on feature hedging, feature absorption, and the Kantamneni et al. finding that low L0 hurts downstream performance; the paper's novelty is primarily the specific decoder-projection diagnostic and the toy-model illustration, which is a relatively incremental addition given the existing literature it builds on.

Presentation issues reduce reproducibility and polish: the 'Our code is available at' sentence is left incomplete with no link, key experimental details (e.g., exact dictionary width scaling with L0 in the toy model, number of seeds, variance across runs) are missing, and several figures (e.g., Fig. 1, Fig. 3) are small and hard to parse without zooming.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored question: whether L0 is truly a free 'sparsity-reconstruction tradeoff' parameter or whether it has a 'correct' value for a given data distribution.

Clean, well-designed toy model with known ground-truth features and correlations, allowing direct visualization (via cosine similarity heatmaps) of how incorrect L0 corrupts learned features in both directions (too low vs too high).

Mechanistic explanation for the low-L0 failure mode is compelling and clearly demonstrated: MSE loss actively rewards feature mixing when L0 is too low, undermining the standard sparsity-reconstruction tradeoff framing used throughout the SAE literature.

The proposed Nth decoder projection score is simple to compute and is validated in two independent ways: it recovers the exact true L0 in the toy model, and its optimum coincides with peak downstream sparse-probing performance (over 100 tasks) in a real LLM (Gemma-2-2b).

Practically relevant finding that most publicly available SAEs on Neuronpedia/SAELens use L0 values far below what the paper's analysis suggests is optimal, which could meaningfully influence community practice.

Honest and specific limitations section, and useful supplementary analyses (sparsity-reconstruction tradeoff breakdown, L0 transition during training, attempt at automatic L0 search) that add depth beyond the main 4-page text.
weaknesses: Empirical scope is narrow: only one LLM (Gemma-2-2b), one layer (12), and only BatchTopK SAEs are studied; the claim that findings 'do not expect to be meaningfully different' for L1/JumpReLU architectures is asserted without evidence.

The toy model, while illustrative, is a single random instantiation (one correlation matrix, one firing-probability schedule); no seeds/replicates or variance estimates are reported, making it unclear how sensitive the core findings are to the specific toy setup.

The Nth decoder projection metric requires choosing N, and the paper shows the slope/shape of the curve (and ease of locating the minimum) varies substantially with N; there is no principled procedure for selecting N in practice, which limits the metric's practical reproducibility by others.

The link between minimizing the decoder projection score and the 'true' L0 is established empirically/heuristically rather than theoretically justified, so it is unclear how robust this correspondence is outside the tested settings.

Effect sizes on the LLM sparse-probing benchmark (Figure 4) are relatively modest (e.g., k=1 F1 moves roughly from ~0.74 to ~0.76 across a wide L0 range), raising a question about how practically significant the 'correct L0' difference is relative to noise in downstream tasks.

The proposed automatic L0-tuning procedure (Appendix A.4) is reported to require extensive hyperparameter tuning and work poorly in LLMs, so the paper does not yet provide a turnkey practical solution for practitioners, despite this being the natural actionable takeaway of the work.

The main text is quite short and some important methodological details (e.g., how many seeds per L0, compute budget, statistical significance of F1 differences) are not reported, which could affect reproducibility and confidence in the reported trends.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically important question: whether L0 is a truly free hyperparameter for SAEs, challenging the common 'sparsity-reconstruction tradeoff' framing used throughout the SAE literature.

Toy model experiments are clean and compelling: with known ground-truth orthogonal features and controlled correlation structures, the paper convincingly shows that SAEs at incorrect L0 (too low or too high) mix correlated/anti-correlated features into latents, while the correct L0 recovers ground truth exactly.

The demonstration that a perfect ground-truth SAE can score *worse* on reconstruction than an incorrect, feature-mixing SAE (Fig. 4-5) is a striking and important result that undermines a widely used evaluation practice in the field.

The proposed n-th decoder projection metric (s_dec_n) is intuitive, cheap to compute, and is validated in both toy models (matching true L0 exactly) and two real LLMs (Gemma-2-2b, Llama-3.2-1b), where its 'elbow' roughly coincides with peak sparse-probing performance.

Extensive supplementary analysis (alternative cosine-similarity metric, JumpReLU vs BatchTopK threshold/bias dynamics, L0 audit of open-source Neuronpedia SAEs, L0-transition training experiments) adds robustness and practical relevance, and the audit showing most public SAEs use too-low L0 has direct actionable value for the community.
Limitations and negative results (e.g., automatic L0-tuning via gradient estimation working in toy models but not robustly in LLMs) are reported honestly rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The LLM validation of the central claim relies on indirect proxies (elbow location of s_dec_n roughly matching peak sparse-probing F1) rather than any ground-truth notion of 'correct' features in real models, so the core toy-model finding is not rigorously confirmed at scale; it is essentially a correlational, not causal, validation.

The metric requires choosing n (e.g., near h/2), and the paper acknowledges this choice is largely empirical/heuristic with inconsistent behavior at high L0 across settings (sometimes a clear minimum, sometimes a shallow plateau), limiting its reliability as a general diagnostic tool.

Experiments are limited to a small number of models/layers (essentially one layer each in Gemma-2-2b and Llama-3.2-1b, plus one cross-architecture comparison at layer 12), and the toy models use fairly simple correlation structures (single correlated hub feature, or one random correlation matrix), so generalization to more complex/realistic feature geometries and other layers/models is not well established.

Several explanations for observed phenomena (e.g., why JumpReLU handles high L0 better than BatchTopK, why encoder bias/threshold trends differ) are speculative ('we suspect') and not tested with targeted causal experiments beyond post-hoc correlational plots.

The proposed automatic L0-tuning procedure (Appendix A.6) is reported to work poorly and require heavy hyperparameter tuning on real LLMs, so the paper's practical contribution is currently limited to a diagnostic requiring a manual L0 sweep, which is expensive.
Limited statistical rigor (3-5 seeds), and the paper does not compare against other plausible baselines/heuristics for choosing L0 beyond its own two proposed metrics.
The code availability link is left incomplete ('Code is available at'), raising minor reproducibility concerns.

strengths: The toy-model experiments are clean and illustrative: orthogonal ground-truth features with controlled correlation structure let the authors directly visualize how low L0 causes SAEs to 'hedge' by mixing correlated/anti-correlated feature components into latents, and how a ground-truth SAE can be outperformed on reconstruction by a 'corrupted' low-L0 SAE (Fig. 4-5). This is a genuinely useful counterexample to the common practice of treating sparsity-reconstruction tradeoff curves as a sufficient evaluation tool.

The proposed n-th decoder projection metric (s^dec_n) is a simple, interpretable, training-free diagnostic with a reasonable mechanistic justification (latent decoder vectors that mix multiple true features should have larger projections on arbitrary inputs).

The paper attempts real-world validation by connecting toy-model findings to Gemma-2-2b and Llama-3.2-1b SAEs and relating the metric's 'elbow' to peak sparse-probing performance, which is a reasonable (if imperfect) way to check external validity.

The comparison between BatchTopK and JumpReLU behavior at high L0, and the proposed explanation via per-latent vs. global thresholds and gradient flow to the threshold, is an interesting secondary finding with plausible mechanistic support (encoder bias/threshold trends in Appendix A.10).
weaknesses: The central toy model is quite simplistic and possibly unrepresentative of real superposition geometry: features are exactly orthogonal, correlations follow simple single-hub patterns (one feature correlated with all others) or one randomly generated matrix, and there is no exploration of how more realistic, structured (e.g., hierarchical, non-orthogonal, or graded) correlation patterns would affect the central claims. The paper itself acknowledges this (Appendix A.8) but does not empirically test robustness to more complex correlation structures.

The core proposed metric s^dec_n does not reliably produce a clear global minimum at the 'correct' L0 in the LLM experiments -- the paper repeatedly notes that the high-L0 region is sometimes flat/shallow (Gemma layer 5) and sometimes has a clear minimum (Llama layer 7, Gemma layer 12 with large n), undermining confidence that the metric is a dependable practical tool rather than one that happens to work in cases shown.

There is no ground-truth validation of 'correct L0' in real LLMs (unlike the toy model). The paper equates agreement between the metric's elbow and peak k-sparse-probing F1 as validation, but sparse probing itself is an imperfect, task-dependent downstream proxy (as acknowledged by cited prior work, e.g., Kantamneni et al.), so this is a correlational rather than causal validation of the central claim that L0 determines 'feature correctness.'

LLM-scale experiments are limited to very few layers/models (Gemma-2-2b layers 5 and 12, Llama-3.2-1b layer 7), with no broader sweep across layers, model sizes, or training distributions, which weakens the generality of the claim that 'most commonly used SAEs have an L0 that is too low.' The Neuronpedia L0 survey (Appendix A.7) is suggestive but not tied to per-layer, per-model optimal L0 estimates obtained by the proposed method.

The automatic L0-tuning procedure (Appendix A.6), which would be the most practically useful contribution, is reported to require extensive hyperparameter tuning and does not reliably work on real LLMs, limiting the practical impact of the paper's main proposed tool.

Statistical rigor is modest: most LLM sweep plots use only 3 seeds per L0, and some toy-model plots use 5 seeds; confidence in the sharpness/location of minima (which is central to the paper's claims) is not rigorously quantified.

The paper does not compare against or discuss alternative existing proxies for SAE quality/disentanglement (beyond their own two proposed metrics), nor does it benchmark against other interpretability-oriented SAE evaluation approaches in the literature, making it hard to assess the relative value of the proposed metric.

strengths: Clear, well-designed toy-model experiments with known ground truth that convincingly demonstrate a real mechanism (feature hedging via correlated/anti-correlated features) by which too-low or too-high L0 causes SAEs to mix true features into single latents, rather than relying only on indirect downstream evidence.

The demonstration that sparsity-reconstruction tradeoff curves can rank a known ground-truth SAE as worse than a 'cheating' SAE that mixes correlated features is a genuinely important and actionable critique of standard SAE evaluation practice in the field.

The proposed n-th decoder projection metric (and the alternative pairwise cosine similarity metric) is intuitive, cheap to compute from existing decoder weights, and is validated in multiple settings: small and large toy models, positive and negative correlation structures, BatchTopK and JumpReLU architectures, and two different LLMs (Gemma-2-2b, Llama-3.2-1b).

Practical relevance is bolstered by a survey of open-source Neuronpedia/SAELens SAEs showing that most in-the-wild SAEs use L0 values well below what the paper's analysis suggests is optimal, giving the work direct applicability to practitioners.

Thorough appendix with many supporting ablations (L0 transition-during-training experiments, extended sdec_n plots across many n values, JumpReLU vs BatchTopK mechanistic comparison of encoder bias/threshold dynamics), which strengthens confidence in the robustness of the core finding and shows diligence beyond the minimum needed for the main claims.
Honest limitations section acknowledging restriction to linear features, simple correlation structures, and limited layer coverage.
weaknesses: The proposed sdec_n metric requires choosing n (recommended near h/2) somewhat heuristically, and in several LLM experiments (e.g., Gemma-2-2b layer 5, many n settings in Fig. 17) the metric shows only a shallow plateau rather than a clear global minimum, undermining confidence that it reliably pinpoints the 'correct' L0 in practice rather than just flagging clearly-too-low L0.

All LLM-level validation is correlational: there is no ground-truth L0 for real models, so the central claim that the sdec_n elbow 'coincides with peak sparse probing performance' is suggestive but not a rigorous confirmation that the identified L0 yields genuinely correct/disentangled features; sparse probing itself is an imperfect, indirect proxy for feature correctness.

The toy models use fairly simple, stylized correlation structures (single-hub positive/negative correlations, or one random correlation matrix for the larger model); it remains unclear how well the theory and metric generalize to the richer, hierarchical, and non-orthogonal feature-correlation structures believed to exist in real LLMs.

LLM experiments are restricted to one or two layers per model (layer 5/12 of Gemma-2-2b, layer 7 of Llama-3.2-1b), which is a narrow empirical base for the paper's broad claim that 'most commonly used SAEs have an L0 that is too low.'

The proposed automatic L0-optimization procedure (Appendix A.6) is reported to require extensive, model-specific hyperparameter tuning to work on real LLMs, limiting the near-term practical actionability of the method beyond manual post-hoc L0 sweeps.
The paper states 'Code is available at' with no link provided in the text, raising a reproducibility concern that should be resolved before publication.

The two proposed metrics (sdec_n and pairwise cosine similarity) sometimes disagree with each other or with different k-sparse-probing settings (k=1 vs k=16) on where the optimum lies (Section 4.1/Appendix A.5.2), and the paper does not provide a principled way to reconcile this, leaving some ambiguity in how practitioners should apply the method.
